headline: Agent authority rails become the transaction network after AI.
exposed: Payment networks, issuer processors, merchant acquirers, cloud agent platforms, identity vendors, and enterprise risk teams that expect agents to move money or make commitments.
decision_changed: Payment and identity roadmap priorities shift from human checkout UX toward agent-specific credentials, programmable limits, merchant trust signals, and liability handling.
watch: Watch for two major card networks, processors, or cloud providers reporting production agent credential volume, not just pilots, and for procurement language requiring distinct credentials for autonomous software actors.
metric: Count of payment, identity, or cloud platforms operating agent credential networks; transaction volume through agent-specific credentials; procurement or regulatory text requiring agent identity and delegated authority for high-value actions.
kill: Kill if by 2031 agents still transact at scale through ordinary user credentials, API keys, or human-initiated payment flows with no separate agent identity, permission, or liability layer.
winners: Mastercard and Visa; Cloudflare, Stripe, Adyen, and identity vendors; Agent runtime and policy-control startups
losers: Closed single-app agent stores; Unlogged consumer-agent apps; Merchants without agent-readable inventory and policy interfaces

headline: Liability moves to the evidence recorder.
exposed: AI assurance firms, cyber insurers, regulated enterprises, autonomous vehicle and robotics operators, healthcare AI vendors, and enterprise legal teams.
decision_changed: AI compliance budgets shift from one-off model evaluations to persistent logging, forensic replay, evidence retention, and independent assurance.
watch: Watch insurance questionnaires and regulated-sector procurement templates for mandatory AI action-log, incident replay, and retention language.
metric: Number of G7 or EU-regulated sectors requiring AI action logs or incident records for legal defense, incident reporting, market access, or insurance coverage; policy wording requiring AI event records.
kill: Kill if by 2031 serious AI incidents are still litigated mainly through ordinary negligence discovery and logs remain voluntary internal telemetry with no sector-specific effect on insurance, legal defense, or market access.
winners: Audit and assurance providers; Security observability and data-retention vendors; Insurers with AI-specific underwriting data
losers: Model vendors with opaque tool execution; Enterprises that treat AI logs as optional telemetry; Generic GRC vendors without runtime data

headline: Autonomous labs bottleneck on standards before autonomy.
exposed: National labs, pharma R&D operations, materials companies, analytical-instrument vendors, lab automation vendors, and cloud scientific-workflow platforms.
decision_changed: R&D infrastructure budgets shift from isolated robot workcells toward interoperable lab operating systems, data schemas, and integration standards.
watch: Watch DOE, NSF, NIST, pharma, and materials RFPs for named requirements around sample management, instrument communication, data management, and model integration standards.
metric: Public procurements or funding programs above $25 million requiring named autonomous-lab standards; industrial contracts requiring standards for sample handling, instrument communication, data management, and model integration.
kill: Kill if by 2031 major autonomous-lab deployments remain dominated by bespoke vendor stacks with no named protocol, sample, data, or instrument standards required in public procurements or industrial contracts.
winners: NIST-aligned standards consortia and national lab networks; Thermo Fisher, Danaher, Agilent, Waters, Bruker, and automation vendors; Lab orchestration software providers
losers: Closed bespoke self-driving-lab stacks; Pure model-discovery startups; Manual CRO workflows without machine-readable provenance

headline: Materials discovery becomes a qualification-data business.
exposed: Battery, aerospace, semiconductor, catalyst, energy equipment, and advanced-manufacturing firms evaluating AI-generated material candidates.
decision_changed: R&D budgets shift from model-only discovery tools toward reliability testbeds, reference datasets, and standards participation.
watch: Watch public postmortems of AI-materials programs for phrases like lifetime testing, qualification, design-in delay, field reliability, and accelerated aging.
metric: Count of AI-discovered or AI-optimized materials missing original commercial design-in targets by at least 36 months due to qualification, reliability, or lifetime evidence; funding or revenue for shared qualification testbeds and data consortia.
kill: Kill if by 2035 three or more AI-discovered materials reach high-volume design-in within 36 months of disclosure without public qualification delays or shared qualification-data businesses becoming material.
winners: Testing labs and standards bodies; Instrument and metrology vendors; Incumbent materials suppliers with field data
losers: AI materials startups with no qualification path; Product teams that accept model confidence as qualification; Commodity data vendors

headline: Programmable-biology access becomes a licensed screening layer.
exposed: DNA synthesis providers, biofoundries, benchtop synthesizer makers, universities, pharma, cloud labs, and institutional biosafety officers.
decision_changed: Biofoundry and synthetic-biology platform budgets shift from raw synthesis speed toward compliance screening, access control, and auditable procurement.
watch: Watch NIH, DOE, EU, OECD, and provider procurement language for requirements around AI-designed sequences, customer verification, record retention, and benchtop synthesis equipment.
metric: Binding US, EU, or OECD screening rules that go beyond simple sequence-identity matching; number of providers selling AI-resilient screening compliance as a paid API or enterprise product.
kill: Kill if by 2030 screening remains mostly voluntary and identity-based, with no broader functional or AI-resilient requirement and no paid compliance API market.
winners: Large synthesis providers with mature screening; Biosecurity screening API vendors; Institutions with strong biosafety procurement
losers: Low-cost synthesis providers without screening; Open benchtop synthesis devices with weak access controls; AI-biology startups ignoring biosecurity workflow

headline: Human causal perturbation atlases become the drug-discovery scarce asset.
exposed: Pharma strategy teams, AI-biology startups, organoid companies, spatial-omics platforms, single-cell technology vendors, and biotech investors.
decision_changed: Business-development teams prioritize partnerships and acquisitions around human perturbation atlases rather than model architecture alone.
watch: Watch pharma BD language for acquisitions or collaborations where the named asset is a human perturbation atlas, organoid atlas, spatial atlas, or virtual-cell training dataset.
metric: Top-20 pharma or mega-biotech deals above $500 million that explicitly center proprietary human perturbation, spatial, or organoid atlases; FDA or EMA approval packages citing such platforms as material mechanism or pharmacology evidence.
kill: Kill if by 2033 fewer than two such major deals are disclosed and approval packages continue relying on conventional animal and in-vitro evidence without atlas-derived human causal evidence.
winners: Single-cell and spatial-omics platforms; Organoid and primary-cell data owners; Pharma companies with proprietary disease atlases
losers: Model-only AI drug discovery vendors; Animal-model-heavy programs in poor-translating diseases; Undifferentiated public atlas mirrors

headline: Grid stability replaces megawatts as the AI load gate.
exposed: Hyperscalers, data-center developers, utilities, battery integrators, power-electronics vendors, grid planners, and infrastructure funds.
decision_changed: Data-center capex moves from lowest-cost megawatts toward interconnection-ready power architecture and utility-approved operating behavior.
watch: Watch NERC, FERC, ERCOT, PJM, and utility filings for mandatory dynamic models, ride-through rules, or BESS/grid-support requirements for data centers above 100 MW.
metric: Number of US RTO/ISO regions or NERC/FERC-linked reliability processes requiring large data-center loads to provide dynamic load models and ride-through or grid-support commitments; GW of AI-campus capacity publicly using BESS, grid-forming inverter, or MVDC front ends as interconnection enablers.
kill: Kill if by 2033 grid operators integrate large AI loads through ordinary substation and capacity studies with no special dynamic-load, EMT-model, ride-through, or grid-support requirements.
winners: Battery and grid-forming inverter vendors; Utilities and RTOs with transparent large-load rules; Power-engineering firms with EMT and large-load expertise
losers: Data-center developers treating power as a commodity input; Regions with opaque interconnection and weak grid models; Generation projects without deliverability or load-integration strategy

headline: AI campuses become heat-sink and water-rights assets.
domain: data-center real estate / cooling / water / heat
exposed: Data-center developers, hyperscalers, district-energy utilities, municipal planners, water authorities, and infrastructure real-estate investors.
decision_changed: Site acquisition and power procurement decisions add heat/water rights as first-order diligence, not late-stage sustainability checks.
watch: Watch >100 MW AI-campus announcements for WUE targets, reclaimed-water agreements, district-heat offtake, and local moratoria tied to water or heat.
metric: Number of OECD jurisdictions requiring new large data centers to reuse material waste heat, use non-potable or closed-loop cooling, or prove infeasibility; share of AI-campus announcements citing heat sink, WUE, reclaimed water, or district-heat offtake as a siting reason.
kill: Kill if by 2032 rules remain disclosure-only and hyperscale AI campuses continue scaling in water- and heat-stressed regions without heat or water constraints materially changing site selection.
winners: District heating operators and municipalities with heat demand; Data-center sites with reclaimed-water rights; Closed-loop and liquid-cooling vendors
losers: Hot, water-stressed data-center markets without reclaimed supply; Developers that secure power before cooling permits; Municipalities giving away heat-sink rights cheaply
